explanations.answer: In the courtyard of the guard
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 2 says Jeremiah was imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, which was in the palace of the king of Judah. Locked up, and the address still has the word PALACE in it. Five stars for the location, zero stars for the stay.

explanations.answer: In the house of Jonathan the scribe
explanations.explanation: That name doesn't show up in this passage, baker. Verse 2 says Jeremiah was imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard, in the palace of the king of Judah. It's an easy one to grab when the options all sound official. Keep that courtyard in your pocket, because it's the spot to remember.

No tower here, friend. The text puts Jeremiah in the courtyard of the guard, and that courtyard is in the palace of the king of Judah (Jeremiah 32:2). Towers sound dramatic, I'll give you that. But this passage keeps him on the palace grounds.

That's it, baker. Zedekiah asks, “Why are you prophesying like this?” and then repeats what Jeremiah says the LORD said: “…and he will capture it.” (Jeremiah 32:3). The king is quoting the message right back at him. Jeremiah is already imprisoned in the courtyard of the guard when Zedekiah says it (Jeremiah 32:2).

Sparing sounds nicer, I know. But Zedekiah's words in verse 3 say the city will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it. Nobody in that verse is offering mercy. Capture is the word to hang on to.

Rebuilding sounds hopeful, friend, but it's not in this message. In verse 3, the city is delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it. Different word, very different day. Later, in verse 15, the passage does say that houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land.
Not quite, baker. The message in verse 5 says that if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will not succeed. So the text says the fighting does not work out. Nobody gets a victory lap in that verse.

Right, friend. Verse 5 says that if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will not succeed. The message says the fighting won't work. It's a hard word, and I think it's not the one Zedekiah was hoping to hear.

Yes, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah that Hanamel will say, “Buy for yourself my field in Anathoth…” (Jeremiah 32:7). The LORD even tells him the cousin is coming before the cousin knocks. That's better notice than I get when somebody says they're stopping by.
Bethlehem is a famous name, so I get the pull, friend. But verse 7 says the field is in Anathoth. Verse 8 adds that it's in the land of Benjamin. Famous town, but not the one on this deed.

SHILOH! Baker, you slammed that answer like a game show buzzer, and my mustache jumped clean off the counter. I respect the confidence, but Hanamel's offer in verse 7 is for his field in Anathoth, and verse 8 puts it in the land of Benjamin. Shiloh never shows up in these verses at all. Anathoth is the name on this deed.

Yes, friend. Jeremiah is the one telling it, and he says, “Then, as the LORD had said, my cousin Hanamel came to me in the courtyard of the guard…” (Jeremiah 32:8). The LORD said he would come, and he came, right to the locked-up prophet. Jeremiah says that's when he knew this was the word of the LORD.

This one is true, baker. Jeremiah is the one telling it, and he says, “Then, as the LORD had said, my cousin Hanamel came to me in the courtyard of the guard…” (Jeremiah 32:8). So the visit happens right where Jeremiah is imprisoned. Hanamel showed up just as the LORD said he would.

explanations.answer: That this was the word of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jeremiah says, “Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.” (Jeremiah 32:8). The LORD had told him Hanamel was coming, and then Hanamel showed up with the request. When it lines up like that, you don't need a second opinion.

explanations.answer: That Hanamel was trying to trick him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, baker. What Jeremiah says in verse 8 is that he knew this was the word of the LORD. Hanamel's visit matched what the LORD had already told him. No trick is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

explanations.answer: That the siege was almost over
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. Verse 2 says Babylon's army was besieging Jerusalem, and nothing here says it's nearly done. What Jeremiah says he knew in verse 8 is that this was the word of the LORD. That's a very different kind of knowing.

Not this time, baker. Verse 10 says Jeremiah signed and sealed the deed, called in witnesses, and weighed out the silver on the scales. Verse 12 adds that the witnesses were signing the purchase agreement. This deal had an audience.

Right, friend. Jeremiah called in witnesses in verse 10, and verse 12 says the witnesses were signing the purchase agreement. It also says all the Jews sitting in the courtyard of the guard were there when he gave the deed to Baruch. That's the opposite of quiet.

That's him, baker. Verse 12 says Jeremiah gave the deed to Baruch son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, in the sight of Hanamel, the witnesses and all the Jews sitting in the courtyard of the guard. Notice how many names the writer included. I can barely fit my own name on a cookie box.
That name isn't in this scene, friend. Verse 12 says Jeremiah gave the deed to Baruch son of Neriah. Then, in verse 13, he gives Baruch his instructions. Baruch is the one holding the paperwork.

Good try, but he isn't in these verses, baker. The deed goes to Baruch son of Neriah, with Hanamel and the witnesses watching (Jeremiah 32:12). Baruch is also the one who gets the next instructions. When the options are all names, the passage is your answer key.

explanations.answer: To preserve them for a long time
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 14 says to put both deeds in a clay jar “…to preserve them for a long time.” The sealed copy and the open copy go in together. Just a jar and a plan that lasts.

explanations.answer: To hide them from the Chaldeans
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what the text says, baker. Verse 14 gives the purpose as preserving the deeds for a long time. The Chaldeans aren't mentioned in that instruction. I'd stick with what the verse says.

explanations.answer: To bury them out in the field
explanations.explanation: The text never says to bury them, friend. Verse 14 says to put both copies in a clay jar to preserve them for a long time. Nothing is said about the field or about digging. Just the jar.

That's it, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “Houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in this land.” (Jeremiah 32:15). Right now there's a siege, and the word is that buying and selling will come back. That's why the jar matters.
That's the opposite of the verse, friend. Verse 15 says houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land. The LORD of Hosts is the one saying it. The word is again, not never.

Rarely is a sneaky one, baker, because it sounds almost hopeful. But verse 15 says houses, fields and vineyards will again be bought in this land. It doesn't hedge or give a number. The promise is plain: again.
